medical.title: Imaging agent may improve diagnoses for rare heart disease
medical.summary: A PET/CT radiotracer demonstrated high sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing cardiac amyloidosis, a rare disease that causes abnormal protein buildup in the heart and heart failure, according to a recent clinical trial published in JAMA.

medical.title: Detecting skin cancer even before it becomes visible with AI-assisted image recognition
medical.summary: Until now, diagnosing skin tumors has relied on detecting visible changes to the skin, and Line-Field Confocal Optical Coherence Tomography (LC-OCT) is a well-established method used for diagnosis. Now, researchers at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU) led by Dr. Moritz Ronicke from the Department of Dermatology at Uniklinikum Erlangen have developed a new approach.

medical.title: When the brain gets tired, endurance suffers
medical.summary: After a day spent perusing reports, juggling emails, resolving conflicts and making decisions, a bike ride will seem more taxing, even though your legs aren't any weaker. To shed light on this phenomenon, Benjamin Pageaux, a professor at Université de Montréal's School of Kinesiology and Physical Activity Sciences, and researchers at Nantes Université tested the effect of mental fatigue on physical endurance. Their study was published in Peer Community Journal.

medical.title: Pacemakers after heart valve surgery have different survival impact by sex, study finds
medical.summary: Following transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI), disturbances in the heart's electrical conduction system can make a pacemaker necessary. A recent study shows that the significance of a pacemaker for subsequent prognosis differs between women and men. Physicians at Karl Landsteiner University (klu Krems) analyzed short- and long-term survival data from more than 1,100 people affected. The analysis revealed clear differences between women and men, suggesting that a more individualized assessment of risks before and after the procedure may be beneficial. This is becoming increasingly relevant as TAVI is also being used more frequently in younger people.

medical.title: Patients with developmental disabilities still face kidney transplant disparities despite state laws
medical.summary: State laws to combat disability-based discrimination in the organ transplant process aren't working, according to new research from The Ohio State University College of Medicine. The study, published in JAMA Internal Medicine, examines national policies designed to help all patients have a fair chance to receive an organ transplant. Despite 40 states passing laws prohibiting disability-based discrimination in the organ transplant process, people with intellectual and/or developmental disabilities (IDD) are still less likely to receive a kidney transplant than those without IDD.

medical.title: This popular fermented food may help flush nanoplastics from the body
medical.summary: A kimchi-derived bacterium can bind to nanoplastics under gut-like conditions and may help carry them out of the body. In mice, the probiotic more than doubled the amount of nanoplastics detected in feces, pointing to a surprising potential use for microbes from fermented foods.

medical.title: Scientists find Ozempic may slow aging itself
medical.summary: Semaglutide helped older healthy mice live longer while improving memory, muscle function, blood sugar control, and several biological signs of aging. Its effects went beyond those seen with calorie restriction, raising the possibility that GLP-1 drugs could tap into a separate biological pathway linked to longevity.

medical.title: Scientists find a way to break pancreatic cancer’s protective shield
medical.summary: Researchers found that blocking IL1RAP could disrupt a powerful inflammatory network that helps pancreatic cancer survive treatment. In preclinical experiments, the approach reduced tumor-protecting cells and fibrosis while boosting the activity of cancer-fighting T cells. That could make chemotherapy and immunotherapy more effective.

science.title: The mosquito's transition from vegan to bloodsucker explained
science.summary: Scents govern most key events in the lives of mosquitoes, and there is extensive research on their sense of smell. A new study reveals how a young female mosquito shifts from focusing entirely on nectar to seeking only blood. An odor receptor that reacts to camphor was found to play a key role.

science.title: How families can support children's early mathematics learning at home
science.summary: For parents whose children have just entered kindergarten or first grade, new fall routines can bring excitement—and some anxiety.

science.title: Earth's chorus waves show limited link to rapid electron loss from radiation belts
science.summary: The Van Allen radiation belts are huge, doughnut-shaped regions of highly energetic charged particles trapped by Earth's magnetosphere. These charged particles play a major role in space weather, so studying them is important for predicting and managing risks to satellites, astronauts, power grids and other infrastructure.

science.title: Sheep grazing may pose greater threat to Scotland's wild pollinators than honey bees
science.summary: Sheep grazing, rather than honey bees, could be the bigger threat to wild pollinators on Scotland's moorlands, according to a new University of Bristol-led study. The research, published in the Journal of Applied Ecology, has found that grazing in spring can remove much of the nectar emerging bumblebees need, while commercial honey bee hives introduced during the summer heather flowering period have a much smaller impact.

science.title: Rice bran—source for antimicrobial, biodegradable food packaging film
science.summary: Rice bran is a plentiful agricultural byproduct that is often underused, but research from the Arkansas Agricultural Experiment Station shows it could be a source of biodegradable food packaging with built-in antibacterial properties.

science.title: Largest dataset of its kind could clarify how massive stars shaped early galaxies
science.summary: The more astronomers learn about the universe's earliest galaxies, the stranger they seem. Many of their surprising properties may be explained by differences between their massive stars and those in galaxies like our own Milky Way. A new University of Utah-led survey with the Hubble Space Telescope is shedding light on the stellar astrophysics operating in early galaxies.

science.title: How amateur naturalists are helping scientists track what everything eats
science.summary: An interdisciplinary team of researchers has created an open-source website for learning what different organisms eat and what eats them. The site—called Who Eats Whom—draws on data from a worldwide citizen science platform and serves as both a valuable resource for ecological research and an educational tool to advance public understanding of the global food web.

science.title: Electrical control method tunes magnetic properties for next-generation spintronic memory
science.summary: A research team led by Professor Jung-Il Hong of the Department of Physics and Chemistry at DGIST has successfully used current pulses to alter the spin configuration within a ferrimagnetic material, lowering its "compensation temperature"—the temperature at which opposing magnetizations cancel each other out—by up to approximately 110 K.

science.title: What billiard balls reveal about computers and the limits of prediction
science.summary: When is a billiard ball not a billiard ball? When mathematicians get involved and view a popular game as a model computer.

science.title: NASA-Funded Research Finds Complex Life Defying Record Heat
science.summary: NASA-supported scientists have discovered an organism that lives at extreme temperatures previously thought impossible for complex life. High temperatures can cause the destruction of necessary cell components, which is a big problem for cells with complex parts like a nucleus encasing delicate genetic information. In the heated waters of California’s Lassen Volcanic National Park, a […]

science.title: Microcrystal electron diffractometer brings hidden hydrogen into focus
science.summary: Hydrogen—the lightest atom—does the heavy lifting when it comes to important chemical reactions. It can be stored and released as clean fuel, and its movements help catalysts build medicines, fertilizers and materials. One way hydrogen is available for use is through a hydride—a hydrogen (H) atom bound to a metal. Yet with standard tools, this metal-bound atom can be hard to find in the structure.

science.title: VR boosts English vocabulary scores for students with dyslexia, pilot study finds
science.summary: Virtual reality (VR) could be a new tool to help students with dyslexia learn English vocabulary more effectively than conventional instruction alone, according to a pilot study involving 30 learners published in the International Journal of Innovation and Learning. Dyslexia is a learning disability that primarily affects reading and related language skills.

science.title: Antibiotic resistance research calls for tests that reflect bacteria's changing environments
science.summary: The World Health Organization (WHO) regards antimicrobial resistance, including antibiotic resistance, as one of the world's major health challenges. A new fundamental understanding of antibiotic resistance could therefore potentially have a far-reaching impact on global public health, animal health and the environment.

science.title: Briny 'death pools' hold clues to early life
science.summary: The origins of the earliest life on Earth, prior to the rise of oxygen and photosynthesis, remain a mystery. Graveyards in brine pools at the bottom of the Red Sea may hold some answers.

science.title: Astronomers detect radio signals coming from an exoplanet for the first time
science.summary: Exoplanets are exotic worlds orbiting distant stars far beyond our solar system. Ever since the first ones were discovered in the 1990s, astronomers have turned their attention to these distant worlds to understand more about them. Now, for the first time, scientists have detected radio signals coming directly from one of these planets, a massive gas giant named β Pictoris b.

science.title: Day and night get equal billing on Tuesday. A guide to the fall equinox
science.summary: The fall equinox is Tuesday, when light and darkness split the day evenly. It marks the beginning of fall for the Northern Hemisphere and the beginning of spring in the Southern Hemisphere.

science.title: New statistical methods could lead to more reliable research findings
science.summary: How much can we really trust a measurement? And how much data do researchers need to collect to draw reliable conclusions? Mohammad Reza Seydi at Umeå University has developed and tested new statistical methods to provide better answers to those questions.

science.title: Gold nanoplasmonic chip tracks L-DOPA response in Parkinson's 'mini-brains'
science.summary: Researchers have developed an organoid-on-a-chip technology that verifies the efficacy of Parkinson's disease treatments in real time. The technology combines a stem cell–derived "mini-brain" with a nanoplasmonic sensor engineered to maximize light–matter interaction.

science.title: 3I/ATLAS has an extreme taste for heavy water
science.summary: More and more details about 3I/ATLAS are filtering through the scientific process as time goes on. Our third known interstellar visitor attracted the attention of some of the world's most powerful observatories when it was discovered in July 2025, and some of those telescopes found something peculiar—the isotopes it contained appeared different. A new paper submitted to The Astrophysical Journal Letters (and available as a preprint on arXiv) by Kenji Furuya of the RIKEN Pioneering Research Institute in Japan and his co-authors shows that the isotopic discrepancy is likely due to the "low metallicity" of the stellar nursery in which 3I/ATLAS was born.

science.title: NASA’s Chandra Finds Unusual Objects in Pinwheel Galaxy
science.summary: Using NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory, researchers found mysterious objects that give off unusually low-energy X-rays but intense levels of ultraviolet radiation. One of the galaxies they studied, M101, is pictured here in this image released on Sept. 9, 2026. Astronomers suggest these newly spotted objects in other galaxies may help solve not one, but two […]

science.title: Can a long-lived seabird evolve fast enough to avoid extinction under a changing climate?
science.summary: As the climate changes, species face a critical question: Can they evolve quickly enough to keep pace with their changing environment?

science.title: The tilt in Earth's axis makes the apparent position of continents shift with the seasons
science.summary: Most kids learn in elementary school that the seasons are caused by Earth rotating on a tilted axis during its yearly orbit around the sun. The substantial tilt, about 23.5 degrees, is thought to be the result of an ancient planetary body, Theia, smashing into Earth about 4.5 billion years ago, in the same cataclysmic collision that formed the moon.

science.title: NASA Astronaut to Answer Questions from New Hampshire Students
science.summary: Editor’s Note: This feature was updated Sept. 22, 2026, to note the time change for the in-flight call with students. Students in New Hampshire will hear from NASA astronaut Anil Menon as he answers prerecorded STEM questions while aboard the International Space Station. The Earth-to-space call will begin at 11:40 a.m. EDT Thursday, Sept. 24, and […]

environment.title: Indigenous land back in Chile brings mixed bag of environmental outcomes: Study
environment.summary: Indigenous land restitution in Chile came with a mixed bag of environmental outcomes and did not boost natural forest cover, according to a new study published in Nature Sustainability. While the return of ancestral lands gave the Indigenous Mapuche communities in southern Chile greater control over how their land was used — leading to an […]

environment.title: 1.4-million-year-old footprints reveal a surprisingly large human relative
environment.summary: Ancient footprints in Kenya reveal that eight Paranthropus boisei may have traveled together 1.4 million years ago, with some individuals reaching surprisingly large, human-like body sizes. The tracks offer a rare glimpse of their social behavior and suggest these extinct human relatives may have lived in more complex groups than previously thought.

environment.title: Seven new frog species were hiding beneath Madagascar’s forest floor
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered seven new species of Madagascar’s elusive diamond frogs, using DNA from modern and century-old museum specimens to solve a long-running biological puzzle. The findings reveal surprising hidden diversity and could help protect these little-known amphibians as their forest habitats disappear.

environment.title: Ancient Egyptian princesses were buried with weapons. Their bones reveal why
environment.summary: Weapons buried with ancient Egyptian princesses may have been more than ceremonial decorations. Researchers studying royal mummies from Dahshur found bone changes consistent with years of archery and other strenuous weapon use. Several women also showed evidence of healed injuries, suggesting surprisingly active lifestyles that may have included hunting or military training.

environment.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
environment.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

environment.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
environment.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

environment.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
environment.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

environment.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
environment.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.

mix_items.title: The mosquito's transition from vegan to bloodsucker explained
mix_items.summary: Scents govern most key events in the lives of mosquitoes, and there is extensive research on their sense of smell. A new study reveals how a young female mosquito shifts from focusing entirely on nectar to seeking only blood. An odor receptor that reacts to camphor was found to play a key role.

mix_items.title: Earth's chorus waves show limited link to rapid electron loss from radiation belts
mix_items.summary: The Van Allen radiation belts are huge, doughnut-shaped regions of highly energetic charged particles trapped by Earth's magnetosphere. These charged particles play a major role in space weather, so studying them is important for predicting and managing risks to satellites, astronauts, power grids and other infrastructure.

mix_items.title: Sheep grazing may pose greater threat to Scotland's wild pollinators than honey bees
mix_items.summary: Sheep grazing, rather than honey bees, could be the bigger threat to wild pollinators on Scotland's moorlands, according to a new University of Bristol-led study. The research, published in the Journal of Applied Ecology, has found that grazing in spring can remove much of the nectar emerging bumblebees need, while commercial honey bee hives introduced during the summer heather flowering period have a much smaller impact.

mix_items.title: Rice bran—source for antimicrobial, biodegradable food packaging film
mix_items.summary: Rice bran is a plentiful agricultural byproduct that is often underused, but research from the Arkansas Agricultural Experiment Station shows it could be a source of biodegradable food packaging with built-in antibacterial properties.

mix_items.title: Largest dataset of its kind could clarify how massive stars shaped early galaxies
mix_items.summary: The more astronomers learn about the universe's earliest galaxies, the stranger they seem. Many of their surprising properties may be explained by differences between their massive stars and those in galaxies like our own Milky Way. A new University of Utah-led survey with the Hubble Space Telescope is shedding light on the stellar astrophysics operating in early galaxies.

mix_items.title: How amateur naturalists are helping scientists track what everything eats
mix_items.summary: An interdisciplinary team of researchers has created an open-source website for learning what different organisms eat and what eats them. The site—called Who Eats Whom—draws on data from a worldwide citizen science platform and serves as both a valuable resource for ecological research and an educational tool to advance public understanding of the global food web.

mix_items.title: Electrical control method tunes magnetic properties for next-generation spintronic memory
mix_items.summary: A research team led by Professor Jung-Il Hong of the Department of Physics and Chemistry at DGIST has successfully used current pulses to alter the spin configuration within a ferrimagnetic material, lowering its "compensation temperature"—the temperature at which opposing magnetizations cancel each other out—by up to approximately 110 K.

mix_items.title: What billiard balls reveal about computers and the limits of prediction
mix_items.summary: When is a billiard ball not a billiard ball? When mathematicians get involved and view a popular game as a model computer.

mix_items.title: NASA-Funded Research Finds Complex Life Defying Record Heat
mix_items.summary: NASA-supported scientists have discovered an organism that lives at extreme temperatures previously thought impossible for complex life. High temperatures can cause the destruction of necessary cell components, which is a big problem for cells with complex parts like a nucleus encasing delicate genetic information. In the heated waters of California’s Lassen Volcanic National Park, a […]

mix_items.title: Microcrystal electron diffractometer brings hidden hydrogen into focus
mix_items.summary: Hydrogen—the lightest atom—does the heavy lifting when it comes to important chemical reactions. It can be stored and released as clean fuel, and its movements help catalysts build medicines, fertilizers and materials. One way hydrogen is available for use is through a hydride—a hydrogen (H) atom bound to a metal. Yet with standard tools, this metal-bound atom can be hard to find in the structure.

mix_items.title: VR boosts English vocabulary scores for students with dyslexia, pilot study finds
mix_items.summary: Virtual reality (VR) could be a new tool to help students with dyslexia learn English vocabulary more effectively than conventional instruction alone, according to a pilot study involving 30 learners published in the International Journal of Innovation and Learning. Dyslexia is a learning disability that primarily affects reading and related language skills.

mix_items.title: Antibiotic resistance research calls for tests that reflect bacteria's changing environments
mix_items.summary: The World Health Organization (WHO) regards antimicrobial resistance, including antibiotic resistance, as one of the world's major health challenges. A new fundamental understanding of antibiotic resistance could therefore potentially have a far-reaching impact on global public health, animal health and the environment.

mix_items.title: Imaging agent may improve diagnoses for rare heart disease
mix_items.summary: A PET/CT radiotracer demonstrated high sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing cardiac amyloidosis, a rare disease that causes abnormal protein buildup in the heart and heart failure, according to a recent clinical trial published in JAMA.

mix_items.title: Briny 'death pools' hold clues to early life
mix_items.summary: The origins of the earliest life on Earth, prior to the rise of oxygen and photosynthesis, remain a mystery. Graveyards in brine pools at the bottom of the Red Sea may hold some answers.

mix_items.title: Detecting skin cancer even before it becomes visible with AI-assisted image recognition
mix_items.summary: Until now, diagnosing skin tumors has relied on detecting visible changes to the skin, and Line-Field Confocal Optical Coherence Tomography (LC-OCT) is a well-established method used for diagnosis. Now, researchers at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU) led by Dr. Moritz Ronicke from the Department of Dermatology at Uniklinikum Erlangen have developed a new approach.

mix_items.title: When the brain gets tired, endurance suffers
mix_items.summary: After a day spent perusing reports, juggling emails, resolving conflicts and making decisions, a bike ride will seem more taxing, even though your legs aren't any weaker. To shed light on this phenomenon, Benjamin Pageaux, a professor at Université de Montréal's School of Kinesiology and Physical Activity Sciences, and researchers at Nantes Université tested the effect of mental fatigue on physical endurance. Their study was published in Peer Community Journal.

mix_items.title: Astronomers detect radio signals coming from an exoplanet for the first time
mix_items.summary: Exoplanets are exotic worlds orbiting distant stars far beyond our solar system. Ever since the first ones were discovered in the 1990s, astronomers have turned their attention to these distant worlds to understand more about them. Now, for the first time, scientists have detected radio signals coming directly from one of these planets, a massive gas giant named β Pictoris b.

mix_items.title: Day and night get equal billing on Tuesday. A guide to the fall equinox
mix_items.summary: The fall equinox is Tuesday, when light and darkness split the day evenly. It marks the beginning of fall for the Northern Hemisphere and the beginning of spring in the Southern Hemisphere.

mix_items.title: New statistical methods could lead to more reliable research findings
mix_items.summary: How much can we really trust a measurement? And how much data do researchers need to collect to draw reliable conclusions? Mohammad Reza Seydi at Umeå University has developed and tested new statistical methods to provide better answers to those questions.

mix_items.title: Gold nanoplasmonic chip tracks L-DOPA response in Parkinson's 'mini-brains'
mix_items.summary: Researchers have developed an organoid-on-a-chip technology that verifies the efficacy of Parkinson's disease treatments in real time. The technology combines a stem cell–derived "mini-brain" with a nanoplasmonic sensor engineered to maximize light–matter interaction.

mix_items.title: 3I/ATLAS has an extreme taste for heavy water
mix_items.summary: More and more details about 3I/ATLAS are filtering through the scientific process as time goes on. Our third known interstellar visitor attracted the attention of some of the world's most powerful observatories when it was discovered in July 2025, and some of those telescopes found something peculiar—the isotopes it contained appeared different. A new paper submitted to The Astrophysical Journal Letters (and available as a preprint on arXiv) by Kenji Furuya of the RIKEN Pioneering Research Institute in Japan and his co-authors shows that the isotopic discrepancy is likely due to the "low metallicity" of the stellar nursery in which 3I/ATLAS was born.

mix_items.title: NASA’s Chandra Finds Unusual Objects in Pinwheel Galaxy
mix_items.summary: Using NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory, researchers found mysterious objects that give off unusually low-energy X-rays but intense levels of ultraviolet radiation. One of the galaxies they studied, M101, is pictured here in this image released on Sept. 9, 2026. Astronomers suggest these newly spotted objects in other galaxies may help solve not one, but two […]

mix_items.title: Can a long-lived seabird evolve fast enough to avoid extinction under a changing climate?
mix_items.summary: As the climate changes, species face a critical question: Can they evolve quickly enough to keep pace with their changing environment?

mix_items.title: Pacemakers after heart valve surgery have different survival impact by sex, study finds
mix_items.summary: Following transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI), disturbances in the heart's electrical conduction system can make a pacemaker necessary. A recent study shows that the significance of a pacemaker for subsequent prognosis differs between women and men. Physicians at Karl Landsteiner University (klu Krems) analyzed short- and long-term survival data from more than 1,100 people affected. The analysis revealed clear differences between women and men, suggesting that a more individualized assessment of risks before and after the procedure may be beneficial. This is becoming increasingly relevant as TAVI is also being used more frequently in younger people.

mix_items.title: Patients with developmental disabilities still face kidney transplant disparities despite state laws
mix_items.summary: State laws to combat disability-based discrimination in the organ transplant process aren't working, according to new research from The Ohio State University College of Medicine. The study, published in JAMA Internal Medicine, examines national policies designed to help all patients have a fair chance to receive an organ transplant. Despite 40 states passing laws prohibiting disability-based discrimination in the organ transplant process, people with intellectual and/or developmental disabilities (IDD) are still less likely to receive a kidney transplant than those without IDD.

mix_items.title: The tilt in Earth's axis makes the apparent position of continents shift with the seasons
mix_items.summary: Most kids learn in elementary school that the seasons are caused by Earth rotating on a tilted axis during its yearly orbit around the sun. The substantial tilt, about 23.5 degrees, is thought to be the result of an ancient planetary body, Theia, smashing into Earth about 4.5 billion years ago, in the same cataclysmic collision that formed the moon.

mix_items.title: Indigenous land back in Chile brings mixed bag of environmental outcomes: Study
mix_items.summary: Indigenous land restitution in Chile came with a mixed bag of environmental outcomes and did not boost natural forest cover, according to a new study published in Nature Sustainability. While the return of ancestral lands gave the Indigenous Mapuche communities in southern Chile greater control over how their land was used — leading to an […]

mix_items.title: This popular fermented food may help flush nanoplastics from the body
mix_items.summary: A kimchi-derived bacterium can bind to nanoplastics under gut-like conditions and may help carry them out of the body. In mice, the probiotic more than doubled the amount of nanoplastics detected in feces, pointing to a surprising potential use for microbes from fermented foods.

mix_items.title: Scientists find Ozempic may slow aging itself
mix_items.summary: Semaglutide helped older healthy mice live longer while improving memory, muscle function, blood sugar control, and several biological signs of aging. Its effects went beyond those seen with calorie restriction, raising the possibility that GLP-1 drugs could tap into a separate biological pathway linked to longevity.

mix_items.title: Scientists find a way to break pancreatic cancer’s protective shield
mix_items.summary: Researchers found that blocking IL1RAP could disrupt a powerful inflammatory network that helps pancreatic cancer survive treatment. In preclinical experiments, the approach reduced tumor-protecting cells and fibrosis while boosting the activity of cancer-fighting T cells. That could make chemotherapy and immunotherapy more effective.

mix_items.title: 1.4-million-year-old footprints reveal a surprisingly large human relative
mix_items.summary: Ancient footprints in Kenya reveal that eight Paranthropus boisei may have traveled together 1.4 million years ago, with some individuals reaching surprisingly large, human-like body sizes. The tracks offer a rare glimpse of their social behavior and suggest these extinct human relatives may have lived in more complex groups than previously thought.

mix_items.title: Seven new frog species were hiding beneath Madagascar’s forest floor
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered seven new species of Madagascar’s elusive diamond frogs, using DNA from modern and century-old museum specimens to solve a long-running biological puzzle. The findings reveal surprising hidden diversity and could help protect these little-known amphibians as their forest habitats disappear.

mix_items.title: Ancient Egyptian princesses were buried with weapons. Their bones reveal why
mix_items.summary: Weapons buried with ancient Egyptian princesses may have been more than ceremonial decorations. Researchers studying royal mummies from Dahshur found bone changes consistent with years of archery and other strenuous weapon use. Several women also showed evidence of healed injuries, suggesting surprisingly active lifestyles that may have included hunting or military training.

mix_items.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
mix_items.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

mix_items.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
mix_items.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

mix_items.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
mix_items.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

mix_items.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
mix_items.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.
